snippet.title: Supply Chain Management Systems Explained | What Is SCM?
snippet.description:
A Supply Chain Management System, or SCM system, helps businesses manage suppliers, inventory, production, warehouses, and delivery.

In this lecture, we explain how SCM systems improve coordination, reduce delays, and control the movement of goods.

What Is an SCM System?
An SCM system is an Information System used to manage the flow of products, materials, information, and finances across the supply chain.
It connects different stages from the supplier to the final customer.

Main Parts of SCM
• suppliers
• purchasing
• inventory
• production
• warehouses
• transport and delivery

How SCM Systems Work
SCM systems collect and share information across the supply chain.
They help businesses:
• track stock levels
• manage supplier orders
• plan production
• monitor shipments
• predict customer demand

Example of SCM
A supermarket can use an SCM system to:
• monitor product sales
• identify low stock
• order from suppliers
• track warehouse inventory
• schedule store deliveries

This helps prevent shortages and overstocking.
Benefits of SCM Systems
• reduces delays
• improves inventory control
• lowers operating costs
• improves supplier coordination
• increases delivery accuracy

Limitations of SCM Systems
• incorrect data causes planning problems
• implementation may be expensive
• supplier systems may not connect easily
• disruptions can affect the entire chain
• cybersecurity risks must be managed

SCM vs ERP
SCM focuses mainly on the movement of goods, materials, and supply chain information.
ERP manages wider internal business operations.
SCM connects the supply chain.
ERP connects the organisation.

The Real Shift
• from isolated suppliers → connected networks
• from manual stock checks → real-time inventory
• from reacting to shortages → demand planning
• from delivery delays → coordinated logistics

Reality Check
• SCM systems cannot prevent every disruption
• poor forecasts can create excess stock
• weak suppliers can affect the entire business
• real-time data must still be accurate

Why This Matters
Without effective supply chain systems:
• stock may run out
• deliveries may be delayed
• costs may increase
• suppliers may receive incorrect orders
• customers may receive poor service

Because at the end:
Supply Chain Management Systems help businesses coordinate suppliers, inventory, production, and delivery from start to finish.

Most world maps use the Mercator projection, which distorts the real size of countries  making places near the poles look much larger, while countries near the equator appear smaller.

In this short, discover why all world maps are technically “wrong” and see the shocking real sizes of countries.

snippet.title: What toys have kids played with throughout history?
snippet.description:
Trace the ancient origins of toys and games throughout history, and discover how play has evolved — and stayed the same.

--

snippet.title: Public Policy Evaluation Explained
snippet.description:
Public policy evaluation measures the results, costs, and impact of government policies.
In this video, we explain why evaluation matters, what governments measure, and how evidence can improve future decisions.

What You’ll Learn
• what policy evaluation means
• how policy success is measured
• why evidence matters

What Is Policy Evaluation?
Policy evaluation is the process of examining whether a government policy achieved its goals.

It studies:
• results
• costs
• wider effects
Evaluation helps governments decide what should happen next.

What Is Measured?
Governments may measure:
• whether the problem improved
• how much the policy cost
• who benefited or was harmed
Good evaluation looks beyond announcements and activity.

Outputs vs Outcomes
Outputs are the immediate activities of a policy.
Outcomes are the real changes produced.
For example, building schools is an output, while improved education is an outcome.

Simple Example
Imagine a government launches a job-training programme.
Evaluation should check:
• how many people found jobs
• whether wages improved
• whether the programme was worth the cost
Training people alone does not prove success.

Types of Evaluation
Evaluation may happen:
• before implementation
• during the policy
• after completion
This helps governments predict risks, improve delivery, and measure final impact.

Why Evaluation Matters
Evaluation can help governments:
• improve weak policies
• stop wasteful programmes
• justify future spending
It also strengthens accountability.

Common Problems
Evaluation may be weak because of:
• poor data
• political pressure
• unclear policy goals
Governments may also ignore results that are politically inconvenient.

Using Evaluation Results
After evaluation, a government may:
• continue the policy
• change or expand it
• end it completely
The decision should be based on evidence, not pride or political image.

Reality Check
Governments often measure how much money was spent or how many activities were completed.
But activity is not the same as impact.

The brutal truth is:
A policy is not successful because government did something. It is successful only if the public problem improved.

Why This Matters
Understanding evaluation explains:
• how policy success is tested
• why failed programmes continue
• why evidence should guide decisions

Because at the end:
Policy evaluation turns government action into measurable evidence and better future decisions.

snippet.title: Corruption in Public Administration Explained
snippet.description:
Corruption in public administration happens when officials misuse authority for personal or political benefit.

In this video, we explain common forms of corruption, why it happens, how it damages public services, and how governments can reduce it.

What You’ll Learn
• what public-sector corruption means
• why corruption happens
• how it affects citizens

What Is Corruption?
Corruption is the misuse of public authority for private gain.

It may include:
• bribery
• favouritism
• misuse of public funds

It can happen at both senior and local levels of government.

Common Forms
Corruption may appear through:
• unfair government contracts
• jobs given through connections
• payments for licences or services

Some corruption is hidden inside normal administrative procedures.

Why Corruption Happens
Corruption becomes more likely when there is:
• weak accountability
• poor transparency
• too much unchecked power

Low professional standards and political interference can also increase the risk.

Simple Example
Imagine a company wins a government contract because it paid an official.
The public may receive poor-quality work while taxpayers pay too much.
The official benefits, but society carries the cost.
Effects on Public Services

Corruption can create:
• poor-quality services
• wasted public money
• unequal treatment

It often harms poorer citizens the most because they depend heavily on public services.

Effects on Government
Corruption weakens:
• public trust
• rule of law
• government credibility

Citizens may stop believing that laws and institutions are fair.

How Corruption Can Be Reduced
Governments can use:
• transparent procurement
• independent audits
• strong penalties

Whistleblower protection and digital systems can also reduce opportunities for abuse.

Reality Check
Corruption is not only caused by dishonest individuals.
It also grows inside weak systems that allow secrecy, political protection, and no consequences.

The brutal truth is:
Corruption survives when the expected reward is greater than the expected punishment.

Why This Matters
Understanding corruption explains:
• why public services fail
• why citizens lose trust
• why accountability systems matter

Because at the end:
Corruption turns public power into private advantage and makes society pay the price.

snippet.title: Components of Information Systems | People, Data, Hardware and Software
snippet.description:
Information Systems are built from multiple connected components.
They do not depend on technology alone.
A successful system combines people, hardware, software, data, processes, and networks.

Here’s the reality:
An Information System works effectively only when all its components support one another.
In this lecture, we explain the main components of Information Systems, how they work, and why organisations need every component.

What You’ll Learn
• the main components of Information Systems
• the role of people in a system
• the difference between hardware and software
• why accurate data matters
• how processes guide system use
• how networks connect users and devices

1. People
People are one of the most important components.
They include:
• employees
• managers
• customers
• system developers
• IT specialists
• data analysts
• decision-makers
People enter data, use information, follow processes, and make decisions.
Without users, even the most advanced system has no practical value.

2. Hardware
Hardware refers to the physical equipment used by the system.
Examples include:
• computers
• servers
• tablets
• scanners
• printers
• smartphones
• storage devices
• payment terminals
Hardware allows users to enter, process, store, and display information.

3. Software
Software refers to the programs and applications that tell hardware what to do.
Examples include:
• operating systems
• accounting software
• customer-management systems
• mobile applications
• payroll systems
• database software
• enterprise systems
Software processes data and helps users complete tasks.

4. Data
Data includes the facts and records collected by an organisation.
Examples include:
• customer names
• sales figures
• employee records
• stock levels
• prices
• payments
• order details
Data becomes useful only when it is accurate, organised, and processed correctly.
Poor-quality data creates poor-quality information.

5. Processes
Processes are the rules, instructions, and steps used to operate the system.
Examples include:
• how an order is processed
• how employee attendance is recorded
• how customer complaints are handled
• how reports are approved
• how data is updated
• how access permissions are managed
Processes create consistency and reduce confusion.

6. Networks
Networks connect computers, systems, and users.
They allow information to move between:
• departments
• branches
• employees
• customers
• suppliers
• cloud platforms
Examples include:
• the internet
• internal company networks
• wireless networks
• mobile networks
• cloud connections
Networks make modern Information Systems connected and accessible.

How the Components Work Together
Consider an online shopping system.

The components include:
• People: customers, warehouse staff, and managers
• Hardware: phones, computers, scanners, and servers
• Software: the website, payment system, and inventory platform
• Data: product details, customer information, and orders
• Processes: ordering, payment, packing, and delivery
• Networks: internet and cloud connections

The system works because all these components interact.

The Real Shift
• from software alone → complete systems
• from isolated technology → connected components
• from raw data → useful information
• from individual actions → organised processes
• from local systems → networked operations

Reality Check
• expensive hardware cannot fix poor processes
• advanced software cannot correct inaccurate data automatically
• untrained employees can weaken the entire system
• weak networks can interrupt operations
• poorly designed systems create frustration and resistance

Why This Matters
Understanding the components of Information Systems helps organisations:
• design better systems
• identify weaknesses
• train employees properly
• protect valuable data
• improve business processes
• choose suitable technology

Because at the end:
An Information System is not one tool—it is a connected structure in which people, technology, data, processes, and networks work together.

snippet.title: India's First Private Gold Mine Is Here | Jonnagiri Gold Project Explained
snippet.description:
India consumes enormous amounts of gold every year, but most of it is imported from abroad. Now, that could begin to change. The Jonnagiri Gold Project in Andhra Pradesh is set to become India's first private commercial gold mine, marking a historic shift in the country's mining sector. But why is this project being called a potential game-changer for India's economy and mineral security?
In this video, we explain how the Jonnagiri Gold Project could reduce India's dependence on imported gold, attract greater private investment into the mining sector, create local jobs, and open the door for gold exploration across multiple states. We also examine why this project is being seen as a proof of concept for broader mining reforms and how its success could reshape India's long-term mineral strategy. Watch till the end to understand why this isn't just about 900 kilograms of gold per year, but about the future of India's resource economy.

snippet.title: Why Government Policies Fail
snippet.description:
Government policies can fail even when their goals are positive.
In this video, we explain how weak planning, poor implementation, political pressure, limited funding, and lack of evaluation can turn a good policy into a failed one.

What You’ll Learn
• why policies fail
• why implementation matters
• how governments can improve results

Poor Problem Definition
A policy may fail when the government misunderstands the problem.

This can happen because of:
• weak research
• incomplete data
• political assumptions
If the problem is defined badly, the solution will also be weak.

Unrealistic Goals
Some policies promise too much in too little time.
Common problems include:
• impossible targets
• unclear priorities
• unrealistic deadlines
Ambitious goals are useless without a practical plan.

Weak Implementation
A strong policy can fail during delivery.
This may happen because of:
• poor coordination
• untrained staff
• unclear responsibilities
Implementation is where policy success is actually decided.

Lack of Funding
Policies need money to work.
Without enough funding, governments may face:
• staff shortages
• delayed projects
• poor service quality
A policy without resources is only an announcement.

Political Interference
Policies may be changed or weakened because of politics.
This can include:
• short-term election pressure
• favouritism
• frequent leadership changes
Political priorities may replace evidence and long-term planning.

Public Resistance
Citizens may reject a policy if it is poorly explained or seen as unfair.
Governments need:
• clear communication
• public consultation
• trust and cooperation
Even a technically strong policy can fail without public support.

Simple Example
Imagine a government launches a job-training programme.
The policy may fail if:
• the training does not match real jobs
• funding is too low
• results are never measured
The programme exists, but unemployment may remain unchanged.

Lack of Evaluation
Governments must check whether policies are working.
Evaluation should examine:
• real outcomes
• costs
• unexpected effects
Without evaluation, failed policies may continue for years.

Reality Check
Policy failure is rarely caused by one mistake.
It usually happens because several weaknesses connect together.
The brutal truth is:
A good idea does not become a good policy until it is realistic, funded, implemented, and measured.

Why This Matters
Understanding policy failure explains:
• why government promises are not enough
• why implementation needs resources
• why evaluation matters

Because at the end:
Policies fail when governments focus more on announcing solutions than delivering results.

snippet.title: Asia's oil scramble is reshaping crude markets, with Lin Ye and Priya Walia
snippet.description:
This episode was recorded on Thursday, 30 April 2026.

Join us for our annual Summits in Singapore, Houston and London: https://rystad.info/4dgjr2q

Let’s Talk Energy and look at how oil-importing countries in Asia are coping with the loss of vital Middle East supply as benchmark prices hit four-year highs above $120. Following the start of the war in the Middle East, many refiners in Asia, who are the largest buyers of barrels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, have spent the two months scrambling to find alternative supplies and bidding up spot cargoes of certain grades. But, at least in one country, that is changing. Recently, China’s refiners have flipped their approach and are selling cargoes back into the market, as export curbs, price controls and price-sensitive consumers hurt the economics of turning the crude into fuel. The change comes at a time when so-called alternative supplies, including those from Russia and Iranian cargoes that had continued to transit until the most recent US blockade of Hormuz, come under increasing pressure. But first, we look at the dynamics surrounding the departure of the UAE from Opec+ and how it could impact the markets in the near-term and further into the future.  

+ How are major Asian importers finding the barrels they need at a price they can afford, while also shielding consumers from higher fuel costs?
+ How has China’s strategic shift impacted both physical and futures markets and how might we expect that behavior to evolve?
+ And will sanctions on one of China’s largest teapot refineries create a bidding war with Indian refiners over a limited available volume of Russian barrels.
